beliefs.practice: Read the cluster connection string only from an environment variable (DOCUMENTDB_URI) at runtime; never hard-code, commit, or log the full URI/credentials — provide a .env.example with a placeholder instead.

Use a short-lived or rotated credential model for the DocumentDB connection (rotate keys or use managed identities / Azure AD where possible) and avoid embedding long-lived keys in app code or containers.
Enforce TLS/SSL for the MongoDB-compatible connection (use tls=true / ssl=true in the connection string) and verify server certificates; never disable certificate verification in production.

Configure client connection pooling (e.g., set maxPoolSize and minPoolSize in the MongoDB URI or client options) and reuse a single MongoClient instance across the application to avoid connection churn.
Enable and handle retryable writes/reads and apply an exponential backoff retry policy for transient network errors (wrap DB ops with retries and Idempotency where appropriate).

Provision and use a single database (sample_fintech_01) and create a dedicated collection for fraud patterns rather than using the default DB or multiple ad-hoc collections; set the collection name explicitly in code and migration/seeding scripts.

Model each fraud pattern document to include: a unique id, a vector field (embedding) stored as a numeric array, metadata fields used for scoring/explanation (e.g., tags, severity, feature-summary), and a timestamp; keep vectors in a dedicated field name like 'embedding_vec'.

When creating a server-side vector index, specify the index type (IVF, HNSW, DiskANN) and concrete parameters: metric (cosine or dot), vector dimension, and an appropriate nlist/M/efConstruction (e.g., nlist for IVF, M/efConstruction for HNSW) — choose parameters based on dataset size and query latency/accuracy trade-offs.

If server-side vector indexes are unavailable, fall back to storing vectors and performing client-side approximate search: pre-filter candidates with indexes on metadata, then compute cosine similarity in the application and keep K small to limit transfer.

Create conventional indexes on metadata and frequently-filtered fields used to preselect candidates for vector search (e.g., transaction type, merchant category, country, time window) to reduce vector search scope and cost.

For vector fields, store the vector as a dense numeric array of floats with consistent dimension; include and validate the dimension at write time to prevent mixed-dimension vectors in the same collection.
Limit returned fields in queries (projection) to only what the scoring/explanation needs (e.g., vector id, metadata, score) to reduce network transfer of large vectors when not required.

When seeding sample data, run idempotent seed scripts that upsert (insert or replace) by a stable key so re-running the seed doesn’t create duplicates; include a `seed_version` or marker in the collection to detect seeded state.
Limit per-document size (avoid embedding large attachments in the same document); keep vectors and metadata succinct and store large blobs elsewhere (blob storage) with references in documents.

When computing a fraud risk score from nearest neighbors, normalize similarity scores to a fixed 0–100 risk scale, document how nearest-neighbor distances map to that scale, and make the explanation derive from the top N matching documents and their metadata rather than raw distances only.

Protect queries from excessive resource consumption: enforce a sensible limit on candidate size (max candidates returned from vector search) and set query timeouts on the DB client so a bad request cannot hang indefinitely.

Use monitoring and telemetry: collect client-side metrics (latency, errors, pool exhaustion) and enable server metrics/alerts for collection RU/IO usage (or equivalent for the managed cluster) to detect hotspots and tune indexes or provisioned capacity.
Use bulk write / bulk upsert APIs when ingesting seed or training data to reduce round trips and leverage server-side batching.

Lock schema expectations in application code/tests (dimensions, required fields, index names) and include unit/integration tests that assert seed-created indexes and collection existence against the live DOCUMENTDB_URI.
Avoid sending raw vectors to logs or telemetry; if you must log vectors for debugging, reduce precision or hash them so sensitive features are not exposed.

When the provider supports server-side vector search, prefer server-side ANN indexes (IVF/HNSW/DiskANN) for production for speed/scale; only use client-side brute-force for small datasets or unit tests.

Apply per-collection throughput or resource controls (or the equivalent cluster-level knobs) so a noisy vector search workload doesn’t exhaust the whole cluster — tune based on observed query profile.
